alternatives.name: Gatus
alternatives.desc: A YAML file, a status board and enough protocol checks to annoy most outages.

facts.install: Run one binary or Docker container and supply a YAML configuration; Helm is available
facts.dataFormat: Monitor definitions live in YAML; results are in memory by default or persist in SQLite or PostgreSQL when storage is configured.
facts.gapVsPaid: It is compact and capable, but lacks the managed multi-region probe network, turnkey escalation, and zero-maintenance reliability of Better Stack or UptimeRobot.
facts.setupBlocker: The first hurdle is writing YAML for endpoints, conditions, alerts, and secrets; without configuring a database, history disappears on restart.

alternatives.name: Kener
alternatives.desc: A handsome status page that also does the checking, not just the apologizing.

facts.install: Docker Compose with Kener and Redis; PostgreSQL or MySQL can replace the default SQLite database
facts.dataFormat: Configuration and incidents default to `./database/kener.sqlite.db`, with PostgreSQL/MySQL supported; Redis carries queues, cache, and scheduled jobs.
facts.gapVsPaid: It is strongest as an attractive status page with checks, not as a mature worldwide synthetic-monitoring and on-call service.
facts.setupBlocker: A usable deployment needs Redis plus a secret key, public origin, persistence, and mail/notification settings, so it is not a one-container static status page.

alternatives.name: OneUptime
alternatives.desc: Uptime, status pages and on-call in one enormous open-source cupboard.

facts.install: Hosted signup, or the release-branch Docker Compose stack; Helm is the production path
facts.engines: Its AI features can connect to OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, Mistral, Ollama, and OpenAI-compatible servers such as vLLM, LocalAI, or LM Studio.
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted telemetry is stored in ClickHouse, application state and configuration in PostgreSQL, and cache, queues, and sessions in Redis.
facts.gapVsPaid: It can replace much of the suite, but doing so means operating a large observability and incident stack instead of buying a small managed monitor.
facts.setupBlocker: The recommended self-hosted footprint is large and production requires secrets, TLS, backups, database care, and frequent upgrades rather than a single lightweight monitor.

alternatives.name: OpenStatus
alternatives.desc: Uptime checks and a status page, with YAML for the suspicious.

facts.install: Hosted signup, or the project's Docker Compose/Coolify self-host stack
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosting uses a LibSQL/Turso-compatible relational database for application state; optional Tinybird stores analytical check data, with mounted volumes for local services.
facts.gapVsPaid: It is a close open alternative, but its global-check coverage, incident ecosystem, and operational maturity remain thinner than the established paid services.
facts.setupBlocker: The full self-host path is several services, not one monitor, including migrations, workflows, API, dashboard, status-page frontend, checker/private locations, database, and authentication/email secrets.

alternatives.name: Uptime Kuma
alternatives.desc: A cheerful dashboard for asking URLs whether they are dead yet.

facts.install: Docker Compose with a persistent `/app/data` volume, or a manual Node.js plus PM2 install
facts.dataFormat: Monitor configuration, users, status pages, certificates, and history live in the application database under the mounted `/app/data` directory.
facts.gapVsPaid: It is simple and friendly, but checks originate from infrastructure you operate and there is no managed multi-region fleet or full on-call service.
facts.setupBlocker: It still needs an always-on host, Docker volume discipline, and outbound notification credentials; network filesystems are explicitly unsupported for the data directory.

prompt:
Build me an uptime monitor like UptimeRobot. Requirements:

- A config file (monitors.json) listing URLs with: name, interval seconds,
  timeout, expected status code, and an optional keyword the body must contain.
- A single long-running Node or Python process that checks each monitor on its
  interval, records results (SQLite: timestamp, status, latency ms), and tracks
  state transitions.
- On DOWN or RECOVERED transitions (after 2 consecutive fails to avoid flaps):
  send a webhook (Discord/Slack/Telegram format, URL from .env) with the monitor
  name, error, and duration of the outage.
- A public /status page: green/red per monitor, uptime % over 24h/7d/30d, and a
  latency sparkline drawn as inline SVG. Auto-refresh every 30s.
- Keep 90 days of history, prune older rows daily.
- One process, no queue, no Docker required; systemd unit file included.
